coach.board: The graph shows commits and branches. The panels show your working tree, the GitHub pull requests and the goals.
coach.actions: Wait lets time pass for a review. Everything else you do in the terminal or the file editor; reading is free, changing costs a step.
coach.firstMove: Run git status and git log --oneline --graph --all (both are free), then read the goals.

events.title: Commit message breaks the conventions
events.fix: Write the subject in the imperative mood, under about 50 characters, and say what changed: "Add retry to the fetch client", not "Added" or "fix". The body explains why.

events.title: Conflict markers were committed
events.fix: git add does not check the file. Search for <<<<<<< before you stage a resolved file, or the markers land in the repo and break the build.

events.title: Merge conflict
events.fix: Both sides changed the same lines. Edit the file to what the code should say, delete the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines, git add it, then git commit (merge) or git rebase --continue. git merge --abort or git rebase --abort starts over.

events.title: Force-push without --force-with-lease
events.fix: A plain --force overwrites whatever is on the remote branch, even a teammate's newer push. --force-with-lease refuses when the remote moved since your last fetch.

events.title: History rewritten on a shared branch
events.fix: Every clone of main now disagrees with origin. To undo a bad commit on a shared branch, add a new commit with git revert instead of resetting and force-pushing.

events.title: A force-push destroyed a teammate's commits
events.fix: The remote branch had commits you had not fetched, and --force replaced them. Use --force-with-lease so the push fails when the remote has work you have not seen.

events.title: git reset --hard threw away uncommitted work
events.fix: --hard discards changes in the working tree and index that were never committed. Commit or git stash push first, then reset.

events.title: A commit is no longer on any branch
events.fix: The commit still exists: git reflog lists where HEAD has been, and git branch <name> <sha> brings it back. Before you move a branch with reset, put a branch on the commits you want to keep.

events.title: A code owner approved your pull request
events.fix: CODEOWNERS auto-requests the owners of the files you changed, and with "require review from code owners" their approval is what unlocks the merge.

events.title: Merge blocked: code-owner review required
events.fix: The PR waits for approval from the owner of a path it changes. GitHub requested them when you opened the PR (not for a draft). Check gh pr view, then wait for the review.

events.title: Merge blocked: a required check is failing
events.fix: A required status check must pass before merge. Read gh pr checks, fix the cause on your branch (or rebase onto the fix that landed on main), and push again.

events.title: Branch protection bypassed with --admin
events.fix: An admin can merge past the rules, but the rules exist so a broken or unreviewed change cannot reach main. Fix what blocks the merge instead.

events.title: The pull request is a draft
events.fix: A draft is not ready for review: code owners are not requested and it cannot be merged. gh pr ready flips it and requests reviewers.

events.title: Direct push to a protected branch refused
events.fix: Branch protection requires a pull request, so main only changes by merging a PR. Push your work to a branch and open one with gh pr create.

events.title: Push rejected: the remote has newer commits
events.fix: origin has commits you do not. git fetch, bring them in with git merge origin/<branch> or git rebase origin/<branch>, then push again.

events.title: --force-with-lease refused to push
events.fix: The remote branch moved since your last fetch, so the lease check failed. That is the safety working: fetch, look at what arrived, integrate it, then push again.

events.title: git pull on diverged branches asks how to reconcile
events.fix: Local and remote both have new commits. Choose git pull --no-rebase (a merge commit) or git pull --rebase (replays yours on top, with new commit IDs).

events.title: Squash merge: one new commit on main
events.fix: GitHub collapsed the branch into a single new commit on main. The branch's own commits are not in main's history, so git branch -d calls it unmerged; gh pr merge --delete-branch cleans up.

events.title: Rebase rewrote commits you had already pushed
events.fix: Rebased commits have new IDs, so a plain git push is rejected. On your own branch use git push --force-with-lease; never force-push a shared branch.

events.title: A teammate pushed to origin
events.fix: origin/* in your graph is only your last fetch. git fetch shows what changed before you integrate it.

events.title: CI is failing on main
events.fix: A commit on shared main broke the build for everyone. Undo it with git revert on a branch and a pull request: a new commit that keeps history intact, not reset plus force-push.

levels.title: 1. Everyday flow
levels.blurb: A fresh clone of acme/site. Add a line to README.md that points at CONTRIBUTING.md and ship it the normal way: branch, commit, push, open a pull request, merge it. Reading is free; each change to the repo takes a step.
hints: Look at the terminal and the graph: you are on main, and a pull request needs its own branch.
The everyday flow is branch, edit, add, commit, push, open the PR, merge it.
git switch -c docs/contributing, edit README.md in the editor, git add, git commit -m, git push -u origin HEAD, gh pr create --fill, gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch.

goals.text: The README change is on origin/main
goals.hint: Branch first (git switch -c docs/contributing), edit README.md in the editor, then git add and git commit -m "..." with a short imperative subject.

goals.text: It got there through a merged pull request
goals.hint: git push -u origin HEAD, then gh pr create --fill, then gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch.
git switch main and git pull (gh pr merge --delete-branch already does both).
Commit or restore what is left in the working tree.

levels.title: 2. Behind main
levels.blurb: Your branch feature/retries has an open PR (#7), but teammates merged to main while you worked, and one of them changed the line you edited. Bring the branch up to date (merge or rebase, your call), resolve the conflict in config.yml (ops raised the timeout to 60: keep 60 and keep your retries: 3), and get the PR merged.
hints: Look at the commit graph: main has moved on past where your branch started.
Bring the branch up to date (merge or rebase). The conflict in config.yml has two sides to keep: timeout 60 and retries 3.
git fetch, git rebase origin/main, fix config.yml in the editor, git add it, git rebase --continue, git push --force-with-lease, then gh pr merge.

levels.title: 3. Protected main
levels.blurb: main is protected: a pull request, a code-owner approval and a passing build. Marc's commit on main broke the build. You also committed a typo fix to your local main by mistake, and README.md has half-finished edits. Undo the bad commit without rewriting history, land the typo fix, and lose nothing.
hints: Look at the graph: Marc's commit on main broke the build, and your local main has a stray typo commit.
You cannot rewrite main or push to it. You undo a commit with a new one (revert) on a branch, through a pull request, and you protect your own work first.
Stash the edits, branch the typo fix, reset main to origin/main, revert on a new branch and open a PR, then rebase and merge the typo PR.
